'''''Tropaeolum majus''''', the '''garden nasturtium''', '''nasturtium''',<ref name = GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> '''Indian cress''' or '''monk's cress''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Tropaeolaceae]]. An [[annual plant|annual]] or a short-lived [[perennial]] with disc-shaped leaves and brilliant yellow, orange or red flowers, it is of cultivated, probably [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] origin. It is not closely related to the genus ''[[Nasturtium (crucifer)|Nasturtium]]'' (which includes [[watercress]]).

==Description==
It is a fast-growing plant, either [[annual plant|annual]] or [[perennial]],<ref>{{Citation |title=''Tropaeolum majus'' |date=11 July 2013 |website=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk |url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/tropaeolum_majus.htm |access-date=2021-06-22 |publisher=Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry |mode=cs1}}</ref> with trailing stems growing to {{convert|3-6|ft|m|1|order=flip|abbr=on}}. The [[leaves]] are large, nearly circular, {{convert|3 to 15|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} in diameter, green to glaucous green above, paler below; they are [[leaf shape|peltate]], with the 5–30-cm-long [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] near the middle of the leaf, with several veins radiating to the smoothly rounded or slightly lobed margin.

The flowers are 2.5–6 cm in diameter, mildly scented,<ref>[https://pfaf.org/user/plant.aspx?LatinName=Tropaeolum+majus Tropaeolum majus - L.] [[Plants For A Future]]</ref> with five petals, eight stamens, and a 2.5–3-cm-long nectar spur at the rear. The petals vary from yellow to orange to red, frilled and often darker at the base. The fruit is 2 cm broad, three-segmented, each segment with a single large seed 1–1.5 cm long.<ref name=jeps>Jepson Flora: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Tropaeolum+majus ''Tropaeolum majus'']</ref><ref name=pier>Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk: [http://www.hear.org/pier/species/tropaeolum_majus.htm ''Tropaeolum majus'']</ref>

===Unique effects===

Nasturtium leaves, like some other species, demonstrate the [[lotus effect]], whereby rainwater falling on the surface gathers into globular droplets which roll off the leaf, leaving it dry and clean.<ref>{{cite web |title=Scientific Image - Water Droplet on a Nasturtium Leaf |url=https://www.nisenet.org/catalog/scientific-image-water-droplet-nasturtium-leaf |access-date=23 June 2021 |publisher=[[NISE]] (National informal stem education network)}}</ref>

''Das Elisabeth Linné-Phänomen'' (the Elizabeth Linnæus Phenomenon), named after [[Carl Linnaeus]]'s daughter [[Elisabeth Christina von Linné]] (who discovered the phenomenon at age 19), refers to the appearance of 'flashing' flowers.<ref>H. W. "[http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v93/n2327/abs/093348a0.html Das Elisabeth Linné-Phänomen (sogenanntes Blitzen der Blüten) und seine Deutungen]", ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' (nature.com). Retrieved 4 May 2013.</ref> Especially at dusk, the orange flowers may appear to emit small flashes. Once believed to be an electrical effect, it is today thought to be an optical reaction in the human eye caused by the contrast between the orange flowers and the surrounding green.<ref name="odla-20130429">"[https://sverigesradio.se/sida/avsnitt/185578?programid=1667 Försenad jätteplantering till Malmös schlagerfest, expert varnar för kalkning och kogödsel på påse]", ''Odla med P1'', [[Sveriges Radio]], 29 April 2013. Retrieved 4 May 2013. (in Swedish)</ref>

== Etymology ==
The species was originally called ''Nasturtium indicum'' ("Indian nasturtium") but the plant is not related to the true ''Nasturtium'' genus.

The current genus name ''Tropaeolum'', coined by [[Linnaeus]], means "little trophy". ''Tropaeolum'' is the diminutive form of the Latin {{Lang|la|tropaeum}}, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek {{Lang|grc|τρόπαιον }} ({{Lang|grc-Latn|trópaion}}, "trophy").

The Latin [[specific epithet]] ''majus'' means "larger" (the neuter form of ''major'').<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1845337315 |location=United Kingdom}}</ref>

[[File:Starr-090430-6605-Tropaeolum majus-flowering habit climbing trees-Kula-Maui (24657509090).jpg|thumb|Climbing habit]]
== Distribution and habitat ==
The species is of cultivated, probably [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] origin.<ref name="rhs">Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref> It originated in the [[Andes]] from [[Bolivia]] north to [[Colombia]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

The species has become naturalized in parts of the United States ([[California]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[Pennsylvania]], [[New Hampshire]], [[Massachusetts]], [[Connecticut]] and [[Virginia]]),<ref name=":0">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200012407 Flora of North America v 7 p 166]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants Profile for ''Tropaeolum majus'' (nasturtium) |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=TRMA7 |access-date=2018-03-07 |website=plants.usda.gov}}</ref> as well as parts of Europe and Asia, Africa and Australia.<ref name=":0" /> It is listed as [[invasive plant|invasive]] in [[Hawaii]] and [[Lord Howe Island]], Australia.<ref name="pier" />

== Ecology ==
The garden nasturtium is used as a food plant by the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera|lepidopteran]] species including the [[dot moth]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.naturespot.org.uk/species/dot-moth |title=Dot Moth - ''Melanchra persicariae'' |date= |work=Recording the wildlife of Leicestershire and Rutland |publisher=NatureSpot |access-date=2012-06-21}}</ref> the [[garden carpet]] moth<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.darwincountry.org/explore/003207.html?sid= |title=Garden Carpet Moth and Caterpillar ''Xanthorhoe fluctuata'', Nasturtium |author=Plymley, Katherine |author-link=Katherine Plymley |date= |website= |publisher=Shrewsbury Museums Service |access-date=2012-06-21}}</ref> and the [[Pieris brassicae|large white or cabbage white butterfly]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/profile.aspx?pid=457 |title=Cabbage caterpillars |date=2011-02-22 |website= |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=2012-06-21 |archive-date=2013-02-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130225104049/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/Profile.aspx?pid=457 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Nasturtium @ Cass House Garden, Cayucos.jpg|thumb|upright|Garden specimen in [[Cayucos, California]]|alt=Bright red-orange flower with a yellow center]]

''Tropaeolum majus'' [[cultivar]]s are widely grown as easy annual plants, and will grow in poor, damp soil in full sun. The large seeds are easy to handle individually.

As they do not tolerate heavy frost, in cooler climates they are best sown under glass in heat, and planted out after all danger of frost has passed. Alternatively, as they are fast-growing, they may be sown ''in situ'' after that time.

Many flower colours are available, in the warm spectrum from cream through yellow, orange, red and maroon. Some have highly decorative marbling on the leaves.

The groups Whirlybird Series<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106276/i-Tropaeolum-majus-i-Whirlybird-Series/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Tropaeolum majus'' Whirlybird Series | access-date = 26 December 2018}}</ref> and Alaska Series<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/64998/i-Tropaeolum-majus-i-Alaska-Series-(v)/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Tropaeolum majus'' Alaska Series | access-date = 26 December 2018}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 103 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 26 December 2018}}</ref>

== Uses ==

All of the above-ground parts of the plants are edible.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=124 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref> The flower has most often been consumed, making for an especially ornamental salad ingredient; it has a slightly peppery taste reminiscent of [[watercress]], and is also used in [[stir fry]]. The flowers contain about {{convert|130|mg|oz}} [[vitamin C]] per {{convert|100|g|oz|frac=2|abbr=on}},<ref name=PFAF>{{cite web |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Tropaeolum+minus |title=''Tropaeolum minus'' |date= |website= |publisher=Plants For A Future |access-date=2012-06-05}}</ref> about the same amount as is contained in [[parsley]].<ref>{{Cite journal |author=United States Department of Agriculture Research Service |year=2010 |title=USDA National Nutrient Database for Standard Reference, Release 23 |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/northeast-area/beltsville-md-bhnrc/beltsville-human-nutrition-research-center/methods-and-application-of-food-composition-laboratory/ |journal=[[Agricultural Research Service]] |publisher=Nutrient Data Laboratory}}</ref> Moreover, they contain up to {{convert|45|mg|oz}} of [[lutein]] per {{convert|100|g|oz}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Niizu, P.Y. |author2=Rodriguez-Amaya, Delia B. |name-list-style=amp |title = Flowers and Leaves of ''Tropaeolum majus'' L. as Rich Sources of Lutein|journal = Journal of Food Science|volume = 70|number = 9|issn = 1750-3841|doi = 10.1111/j.1365-2621.2005.tb08336.x|pages = S605–S609|year = 2005}}</ref> The unripe seed pods can be harvested and dropped into spiced vinegar to become a condiment and garnish, sometimes used in place of [[caper]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantea.com/nasturtium.htm |title=Poor Man's Capers: How to make gourmet capers from nasturtium seed pods |author=Owen, Marion |date= |website= |publisher= |access-date=2012-06-24}}</ref>

Some native South Americans used the plant medicinally, apparently due to its [[antibiotic]] (including antibacterial) properties.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Lyle|first=Katie Letcher|title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants, Mushrooms, Fruits, and Nuts: How to Find, Identify, and Cook Them|publisher=[[FalconGuides]]|year=2010|isbn=978-1-59921-887-8|edition=2nd|location=Guilford, CN|pages=130|oclc=560560606|orig-year=2004}}</ref> Some Europeans ate it to treat urinary and genital infections.<ref name=":1" />
